benefits: Instantly decode any cron expression into a field-by-field table with plain meanings.
See the next 5 actual run times, so timezone and schedule mistakes surface before deploy.
Per-field validation pinpoints exactly which field is wrong and why.
Works as the perfect companion to the Cron Builder: build there, verify here.

faqs.a: Five fields: minute (0-59), hour (0-23), day of month (1-31), month (1-12), day of week (0-6, where both 0 and 7 mean Sunday). * means every value, */n means every nth value, 1-5 is a range, and 1,15 is a list.
faqs.q: What do the five cron fields mean?

faqs.a: */15 in the minute field. The parser reads it as every 15 minutes (0, 15, 30, 45) and the next-run preview confirms the spacing. Combine with an hour range like 9-17 to limit it to working hours.

When both are restricted, cron treats them as OR: the job runs when either matches. 0 0 1 * 0 runs at midnight on the 1st of the month AND every Sunday. The field table shows each field's meaning so this stops being surprising.
faqs.q: Why does my job run on unexpected days?

faqs.a: Both 0 and 7 mean Sunday. This parser accepts 7 and shows it as Sunday in the meaning column. Some systems only accept 0-6, so prefer 0 for maximum portability.

Classic 5-field cron has minute precision and no seconds field. If your expression has six fields (seconds first), it is probably Quartz or a Node scheduler format, which this parser does not read. Remove the seconds field to parse the rest.
faqs.q: My expression has 6 fields. Why does it fail?

faqs.a: The preview is computed in your browser's timezone. Servers usually run on UTC, so a job that looks like 09:00 here may run at a different local hour there. Compare against your server's date output when scheduling across timezones.
faqs.q: The next runs look off by a few hours. Why?

cron-parser.formula:
* * * * *
| | | | |
| | | | +-- day of week (0-6, 0 and 7 = Sunday)
| | | +---- month (1-12)
| | +------ day of month (1-31)
| +-------- hour (0-23)
+---------- minute (0-59)

* = every value, */n = every nth value, a-b = range, a,b = list.
Next runs are found by stepping minute-by-minute from now and testing
all five fields (day of month OR day of week when both are restricted).

cron-parser.quickAnswer: Paste any 5-field cron expression and this parser decodes it into a field-by-field table with plain meanings, a one-line description and the next 5 run times. For example, */15 9-17 * * 1-5 means every 15 minutes, hours 9 to 17, every day of the month, every month, Monday to Friday. Invalid fields are flagged by name so you know exactly what to fix.
cron-parser.tagline: Decode any cron expression into plain English, with a next-run preview.
cron-parser.workedExample:
Input: */15 9-17 * * 1-5
Field breakdown:
1. Minute: */15 -> every 15 minutes (0, 15, 30, 45).
2. Hour: 9-17 -> 9 to 17.
3. Day of month: * -> every possible value.
4. Month: * -> every possible value.
5. Day of week: 1-5 -> Monday to Friday.
Description: runs on the schedule */15 9-17 * * 1-5.
Meaning: every 15 minutes between 09:00 and 17:45, Monday to Friday.
The next-5-runs preview then lists the actual upcoming timestamps.
